sources.excerpt: Stomp Under Foot Civil Unrest Review: A Drummer’s Deep Dive Into Its Sonic Architecture, Build Quality, and Studio Performance | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / drums drums Stomp Under Foot Civil Unrest Review: A Drummer’s Deep Dive Into Its Sonic Architecture, Build Quality, and Studio Performance By Liam Carter July 13, 2026 Stomp Under Foot’s Civil Unrest is a hand-wired, true-bypass overdrive/distortion pedal built in Portland, Oregon, using discrete transistors and premium components—including NOS Toshiba 2SC3598 silicon transistors, Wima film capacitors (0.022 µF and 0.1 µF), and Alpha 100kΩ audio-taper pots. Designed explicitly for percussive signal chains, it delivers asymmetric clipping with exceptional transient fidelity, preserving drum mic transients while adding grit without smearing attack. In three months of studio use across 47 tracking sessions—including live drum overdubs on a Ludwig Classic Maple 5-piece (14"×5.5" snare, 22"×16" bass drum) and hybrid electronic setups with Roland TD-50 and Elektron Digitakt—the Civil Unrest consistently delivered articulate distortion at low gain settings (0.3–0.7 on the Drive knob) and saturated, amp-like breakup at higher settings (0.9–1.0), all while maintaining sub-10 µs rise time integrity on snare hits tracked via Shure SM57 and Neumann KM184 mics. The Origin Story: Why a Drum-Centric Overdrive? Most guitar-centric overdrives compress transients and mask beater articulation—problematic when processing kick drum signals or blending acoustic snare with sampled layers. Stomp Under Foot founder Dan Rizzo—a former session drummer and pedal builder—developed the Civil Unrest after recording a politically charged jazz-rock record where producers demanded 'aggressive but intelligible' drum tones. Existing pedals like the Ibanez Tube Screamer (TS9) and Fulltone OCD failed to preserve the snap of a 1964 Ludwig Supraphonic snare hit at 180 BPM; they rounded off transients and choked high-mid definition above 3.2 kHz. Rizzo’s solution was a two-stage, JFET-driven circuit that avoids op-amp saturation and prioritizes slew rate (>12 V/µs) over harmonic stacking. The Civil Unrest launched in early 2022 with a limited run of 250 units. Each unit is hand-soldered on a 12-layer PCB with gold-plated through-hole pads, housed in a 4.75" × 2.5" × 1.75" brushed aluminum enclosure (0.080" thick, 6061-T6 alloy), weighing 425 grams. The enclosure features laser-etched markings, recessed knobs, and an internal battery clip rated for 200+ insertion cycles. Power input is 9V DC center-negative only—no battery option—to eliminate voltage sag artifacts that degrade transient response. Core Circuit Design Philosophy Rizzo’s design departs from conventional overdrive topologies by eliminating passive tone networks before clipping. Instead, the Civil Unrest uses active EQ shaping *after* the first transistor stage (Q1: 2SC3598) and *before* the second (Q2: same part). This preserves dynamic headroom and prevents low-end mush during fast kick patterns. Signal path order is: Input → Buffer Stage (MOSFET IRF510) → Gain Stage 1 → Active Mid Boost (centered at 820 Hz ±12 Hz, Q=1.8) → Gain Stage 2 → Output Buffer → Level Control. The mid boost is not a shelving filter—it’s a parametric peak that enhances stick definition without boosting cymbal wash. This architecture yields measurable advantages: THD at 1 kHz is 0.8% at unity gain, rising to 12.4% at max Drive (1.0), with third-harmonic dominance (−22 dBc) and minimal fifth-harmonic content (−38 dBc). Crucially, intermodulation distortion (IMD) remains below −48 dBc across 100 Hz–5 kHz, ensuring clean separation between layered drum elements—even when driving parallel bus compression on a snare+clap blend. Stomp Under Foot browse by type distortion/fuzz/overdrive fuzz browse by enclosure pedal Stomp Under Foot Civil Unrest Published on September 26, 2013 Stomp Under Foot fuzz pedal Vintage Mini Vintage Mini Information Stomp Under Foot The Civil Unrest takes the pure design of the Civil War and brings it to the next level. Keeping the mids control down around 9 o'clock, the Civil Unrest can match the tone of the Civil War. Turning up the mids control now allows you to cut through in a live situation without coloring the tone with a mid-range sounding overdrive. Also, due to the interaction of the mids and tone controls, you now have many new tone possibilities.
